title: Deep Learning
common_problem: lots of real examples but no equation to predict what comes next
domain: scientific prediction from large measured or simulated data sets
why_it_matters: learns patterns in data when we don't have an equation, but only on examples like the training set
keeps: millions of dials (weights) that wire inputs through layers into a prediction number
leaves_out: why the prediction happened or which physical rule drove it
failure_boundary: works on data it saw during training but breaks on new situations, new boundary, or bigger scale
everyday_anchor: Teaching a computer to predict physics is like teaching a kid to ride a bike on flat ground, then hoping they can ride on hills. Deep learning finds the patterns—the exact tilt angles, speeds, timing—that work on flat roads. But if the hill is steeper than anything they practiced on, they crash. Physics-informed learning is different: it builds in the rule that gravity always pulls down the same way, so the kid knows hills just tilt the same physics they already learned.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks
common_problem: sparse measurements, but the answer must follow known physical laws
domain: differential equations in science and engineering
why_it_matters: the penalty steers the fit toward physics-obeying answers, filling gaps without pretending data alone tells the story
keeps: neural network guess plus a penalty when it breaks the governing equation
leaves_out: wrong equations, bad boundary conditions, sharp jumps in the real answer
failure_boundary: penalty hides small errors near boundaries or sudden changes
everyday_anchor: Teaching a computer to predict physics is usually a choice: follow the raw data you measured, or follow the laws (like gravity) that you know are true. A PINN does both—it fits a curve through your blurry photos of a dropped ball, but the curve must obey gravity at every point. The equation acts as an invisible guardrail that guides the guess into the gaps where you have no measurements.

title: Partial Differential Equations
common_problem: something changes everywhere at once—how do you describe that with math?
domain: fluids, heat, waves, mechanics, chemistry, climate, and other changing fields
why_it_matters: it forces you to write down exactly what you believe before letting data fill in the gaps
keeps: the map of values across space, how they shift moment to moment, where the edges start and stop
leaves_out: things you didn't model, tiny details too small to see, guesses about numbers, rounding errors
failure_boundary: if you ignore the constraints—like how fast something spreads or that nothing vanishes—your prediction breaks down far from the training data
everyday_anchor: Imagine watching ink spread in water: every point gets darker as ink drifts in from neighbors, but the total ink never increases—it just moves. A PDE is the recipe that says how fast and in what direction. If a neural network just watches video of the ink without knowing the recipe, it might predict the ink suddenly appearing in the middle because it never learned the rule that ink must come from somewhere.

title: Operator Learning
common_problem: predict all values (temperature, pressure, flow) across a whole space at all times, for several starting conditions
domain: fast prediction for families of scientific simulations
why_it_matters: trades running expensive equations thousands of times for one fast learned map, but only if new situations match the training data
keeps: a learned function that takes any starting setup straight to the complete answer everywhere
leaves_out: whether the learned answer still works if the space shape changes, or the physics shifts from what it learned on
failure_boundary: the learned map looks reasonable but breaks physics underneath, or crashes when you try a different-shaped container
everyday_anchor: Teaching machines physics means blending known laws with pattern-learning so they predict systems fast without cheating physics. Operator learning is like learning a shortcut: instead of solving a recipe's heat-flow math every time you cook, you once learn the pattern so well you can instantly guess the temperature everywhere in an oven. But your shortcut only works for ovens shaped like the ones you learned from.

title: Scientific Machine Learning
common_problem: teach a program both the data and the physics rules so it predicts correctly on cases it never saw
domain: using data-driven models inside scientific workflows
why_it_matters: when the program learns from both data and equations, it finds the real pattern instead of just memorizing; that real pattern works on new situations
keeps: a program with millions of dials that learns by checking itself against both real examples and physics equations
leaves_out: any physics rule the scientist doesn't write down as an equation—the program only knows what you tell it
failure_boundary: if the equation is wrong or doesn't exist, the program learns the data pattern but not the truth that works everywhere
everyday_anchor: Imagine training a friend to cook by showing them photos of finished dishes AND telling them why flavors work: how salt brings out sweetness, how heat changes texture. The friend learns real cooking rules, not just copy-paste recipes, so they can invent new dishes. Physics-informed machine learning does the same—a program learns from data AND from the equations describing how the world works, so it builds real understanding instead of just memorizing examples.

title: Surrogate Modeling
common_problem: running the real simulator costs too much money or time to do hundreds of times
why_it_matters: answers questions 1000x faster, but only inside the range it saw during training
keeps: what the simulator learned: if you change input X this way, output Y changes that way
leaves_out: all the detailed physics inside; only sees patterns from the training examples
failure_boundary: confidently guesses wrong answers for situations outside its training set, with no warning it is guessing
everyday_anchor: The big picture is teaching computers physics without running expensive experiments every time. Think of it like this: a coach films a few videos of a runner, then writes down the patterns she notices—how leg speed relates to stride length, how body angle changes with terrain. Now the coach can predict how the runner will move across many slopes the camera never filmed. But ask the coach to predict what happens at 100 mph when the runner only trained at 10 mph? The coach's pattern breaks, but confidence sounds the same.

title: Uncertainty And Generalization
common_problem: how do you know when a prediction is trustworthy instead of a blind guess?
why_it_matters: when a prediction affects real people, the program must admit I trained here, not there—most just guess silently and fail
keeps: honest reporting of where the model might break, ranges it learned from, test results on unfamiliar setups
leaves_out: predicting what happens when you push way beyond the conditions the model trained on
failure_boundary: model looks correct on familiar data while it silently gives nonsense in new terrain, new shape, new sensor, or new physical regime
everyday_anchor: A GPS map is only as good as its border: past that edge you are lost. Physics-informed models must do the same—mark exactly where your training data ends and admit when the computer has never seen a situation before. This keeps engineers and scientists from trusting a prediction in regions the model never actually learned.

title: Optimization For Learning
common_problem: the program has millions of dials to turn and needs a way to know which turns make it better or worse
domain: turning model fitting into a repeatable computation
why_it_matters: turning dials to make the number smaller works, but only for things the number measures; if the number ignores heat conservation, the program learns the wrong physics
keeps: a number that measures how far the program's answer is from what should happen
leaves_out: any goal the number doesn't check, even if it's part of the real physics
failure_boundary: the number gets smaller while the program breaks the real physics, because the number never checked that rule
everyday_anchor: Teaching a computer physics means writing down what you want to improve, then letting the program adjust itself to improve exactly that. The catch: if you only score "predict the temperature" but forget to score "obey the law that heat spreads evenly", the program will nail the temperature while inventing fake physics. Optimization is like that rubric—the program learns exactly what you teach it to measure.

title: Generative Modeling
common_problem: need several possible solutions, not just one best guess, to explore what could work
domain: creating plausible scientific samples, fields, or candidate designs
why_it_matters: when you can't list every possible answer, having a program generate many plausible tries helps you explore; but a plausible-looking answer might actually break the physics
keeps: a program with millions of dials it tunes to learn how to make new examples that match patterns in data it saw
leaves_out: no check that made examples follow the physics laws or obey the real-world constraints
failure_boundary: a generated shape looks buildable but would collapse under load; a predicted fluid flow looks smooth and correct but loses mass where it shouldn't
everyday_anchor: When you're baking, a recipe teaches you the pattern of how flour, sugar, and eggs combine to make cookies that taste right. But the recipe doesn't guarantee every batch will actually work if you skip checking the oven temperature. Generative modeling does something similar: it learns patterns from examples to create new possibilities, but those new creations might look right without actually obeying the physics laws that matter for your problem. Teaching generative models to respect physics is what keeps them from generating pretty but broken answers.

title: Graphs And Geometric Learning
common_problem: molecules, proteins, and meshes have a shape and connections that rows of numbers throw away
domain: systems made of interacting parts, meshes, molecules, or spatial relations

leaves_out: distant effects that skip over neighbors, or interactions that only show up when the whole shape bends
failure_boundary: if the graph misses a real bond or connection, or if parts of the shape rearrange and the model sees a stranger structure
everyday_anchor: Teaching a computer physics means giving it the real structure of how molecules and proteins work—not just lists of numbers. Imagine describing a city not as addresses but as a map of which blocks touch and which roads connect them; a graph neural network learns the same way, by seeing each atom's neighbors in a molecule or how protein backbones loop and touch nearby pieces. The shape and order matter more than raw counts.

title: Neural Differential Equations
common_problem: scientists watch a system change over time but don't know the rule driving that change
domain: changing systems where time evolution is part of the model

everyday_anchor: Teaching a computer to predict the weather is like learning to steer a car by only watching tiny increments. Neural differential equations work by learning these tiny stepping rules directly from data, but like the weather forecast, small mistakes avalanche into large ones.

title: Foundation Models For PDEs
common_problem: scientists retrain from scratch for each equation, grid size, and number—duplicating work unnecessarily
domain: broad families of PDE problems and scientific fields
why_it_matters: one shared model costs less to train if it picks up features that matter across many problems, but only if those features actually switch to new situations
keeps: general patterns in how liquids, heat, and waves behave that work across several setups
leaves_out: whether the learned patterns still work for conditions the model never saw during training—like a completely new shape or an extreme case
failure_boundary: model learns the common cases it trained on and breaks when facing rare physics events, unexpected shapes, or starting conditions it never encountered
everyday_anchor: You learn to cook pasta by making it a thousand times in your home kitchen—same pot, same water, same heat. One day you try cooking in a mountain cabin with thin air, and suddenly your timing is all wrong. The foundation model for equations faces the same gap: it learned heat and flow from lots of standard cases, but a new material, an extreme condition, or a boundary it never saw can make it fail completely. What this adds is speed—one model instead of retraining from nothing each time—but that speed only works if nature stays familiar.

leaves_out: connections between parts that the attention pattern skips over
failure_boundary: when attention picks the wrong patches to look at, the model misses real physical effects traveling across the field
everyday_anchor: When a weather forecaster predicts rain over your city, she's not staring at every pixel of the satellite image equally. She spots the ocean temperature 500 miles away and the jet stream pattern another 1000 miles away—those actually drive your weather. Attention does this for a learning program: instead of checking every input, it learns to zoom into the distant parts that truly affect each output, making predictions fast without breaking physics.
